items.name: Andaman Sea
items.text: A marginal sea of the Indian Ocean east of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, with depths of more than 4,000 m.

items.name: Arabian Sea
items.text: About 3.9 million km², with a maximum depth near 4,600 m. Its winds and temperatures drive the Indian monsoon.

items.name: Baltic Sea
items.text: About 377,000 km². A shallow, brackish sea with limited exchange with the North Sea, so it is sensitive to nutrient pollution.

items.name: Bay of Bengal
items.text: Roughly 2.2 million km², the largest bay in the world. It receives the Ganga, Brahmaputra, Irrawaddy and many other rivers.

items.name: Bering Sea
items.text: About 2.3 million km², linking the Pacific and the Arctic through the Bering Strait; major commercial fisheries.

items.name: Black Sea
items.text: About 436,000 km² and up to about 2,200 m deep. Its deep waters contain almost no oxygen.

items.name: Caribbean Sea
items.place: Central America, Caribbean, northern South America
items.text: About 2.75 million km², a warm sea with extensive coral reefs, mangroves and seagrass beds.

items.name: Coral Sea
items.place: Australia, Papua New Guinea, Pacific islands
items.text: Lies off north-eastern Australia and includes the waters of the Great Barrier Reef.

items.name: Laccadive Sea
items.text: The sea off India’s south-west coast that surrounds Lakshadweep and the Maldives, with coral atolls.

items.name: Mediterranean Sea
items.text: About 2.5 million km², linked to the Atlantic by the Strait of Gibraltar, which is only about 14 km wide at its narrowest.

items.name: North Sea
items.text: About 570,000 km² and shallow, averaging roughly 95 m. A major fishing ground and offshore energy region.

items.name: Persian Gulf
items.text: About 250,000 km² and shallow, averaging around 50 m. Very saline and warm, and central to global oil shipping.

items.name: Red Sea
items.place: Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Eritrea, Yemen
items.text: About 2,250 km long and linked to the Mediterranean by the Suez Canal. Known for coral reefs that tolerate warm water.

items.name: Sargasso Sea
items.text: Defined by ocean currents rather than coastlines, and named for the floating Sargassum seaweed that gathers there.

items.name: Sea of Japan
items.text: A nearly enclosed marginal sea of the Pacific with a maximum depth of about 3,700 m.

items.name: South China Sea
items.text: About 3.5 million km², one of the busiest shipping routes in the world; maritime boundaries are disputed.

items.name: Tasman Sea
items.text: The part of the south-west Pacific between Australia and New Zealand.

items.name: Arctic Ocean
items.text: About 14.1 million km². The smallest and shallowest ocean, largely covered by sea ice and bordered by Russia, Norway, Greenland, Canada and the United States.

items.name: Atlantic Ocean
items.text: About 106 million km². Split by the Mid-Atlantic Ridge; its deepest point, in the Puerto Rico Trench, is roughly 8,400 m.

items.name: Indian Ocean
items.text: About 70.6 million km². Drives the South Asian monsoon; deepest point is in the Java Trench, roughly 7,300 m.

items.name: Pacific Ocean
items.text: About 165 million km². The largest and deepest ocean; Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is roughly 10,900 m deep.

items.name: Southern Ocean
items.text: About 21.9 million km². Circles Antarctica and carries the Antarctic Circumpolar Current. Treated as a distinct ocean by the IHO since 2000 and by National Geographic since 2021.

items.name: Amazon River
items.text: About 6,400 km. Carries the largest discharge of any river, around 209,000 m³/s.

items.name: Congo River
items.text: About 4,700 km. The deepest known river, with depths beyond 220 m.

items.name: Danube
items.text: About 2,850 km. Flows through or along the border of ten countries to the Black Sea.

items.name: Ganga (Ganges)
items.text: About 2,525 km. Rises at Gangotri and reaches the Bay of Bengal, forming the Sundarbans delta with the Brahmaputra.

items.name: Godavari
items.text: About 1,465 km. The longest river of peninsular India and the second longest in India after the Ganga.

items.name: Mahanadi
items.text: About 858 km. Rises in Chhattisgarh and is dammed at Hirakud before reaching the Bay of Bengal.

items.name: Mekong
items.text: About 4,350 km. Flows from the Tibetan Plateau through six countries to Vietnam.

items.name: Mississippi–Missouri
items.text: About 6,275 km combined. The main river system of the United States, draining into the Gulf of Mexico.

items.name: Nile
items.text: About 6,650 km. Often cited as the longest river; its basin covers eleven countries. Length versus the Amazon is debated.

items.name: Volga
items.text: About 3,530 km. The longest river in Europe, flowing into the Caspian Sea.

items.name: Yangtze
items.text: About 6,300 km. The longest river in Asia, flowing entirely within China.

items.name: Brahmaputra
items.text: About 2,900 km in total. Rises in Tibet as the Yarlung Tsangpo and flows through Arunachal Pradesh and Assam before joining the Ganga delta.

items.name: Chambal
items.text: About 960 km. A Yamuna tributary through Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, known for its ravines and a protected gharial sanctuary.

items.name: Indus
items.text: About 3,180 km in total, flowing from Tibet through Ladakh and Pakistan to the Arabian Sea. Its basin supports the Indus irrigation system.

items.name: Kaveri (Cauvery)
items.text: About 800 km from the Western Ghats in Karnataka to the Bay of Bengal in Tamil Nadu; the subject of a long-running water-sharing dispute.

items.name: Krishna
items.text: About 1,400 km from the Western Ghats in Maharashtra through Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh to the Bay of Bengal.

items.name: Narmada
items.text: About 1,312 km, flowing west through Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat to the Arabian Sea, unlike most peninsular rivers.

items.name: Tapti
items.text: About 724 km, flowing west through Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat to the Arabian Sea.

items.name: Yamuna
items.text: About 1,376 km. The largest tributary of the Ganga, rising at Yamunotri and joining it at Prayagraj.

items.name: Caspian Sea
items.text: About 371,000 km². The largest inland body of water; salinity is roughly a third of ocean water.

items.name: Chilika Lake
items.text: A large brackish-water lagoon on the Bay of Bengal coast and a Ramsar wetland, known for wintering waterbirds.

items.name: Dead Sea
items.text: Shoreline about 430 m below sea level, the lowest land elevation on Earth. Hypersaline and shrinking.

items.name: Lake Baikal
items.text: Deepest lake at about 1,642 m and among the oldest, with roughly a fifth of the world’s unfrozen surface fresh water.

items.name: Lake Superior
items.text: About 82,100 km². The largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area.

items.name: Lake Tanganyika
items.text: About 1,470 m deep, the second deepest lake, and the longest freshwater lake at roughly 673 km.

items.name: Lake Titicaca
items.text: At about 3,810 m, the highest large navigable lake in the world.

items.name: Lake Victoria
items.text: About 68,800 km². Africa’s largest lake and a source of the White Nile.

items.name: Wular Lake
items.text: One of Asia’s largest freshwater lakes and a Ramsar wetland.

items.name: Achanakmar Wildlife Sanctuary
items.text: Part of the Achanakmar–Amarkantak Biosphere Reserve; forest habitat that supports tigers and leopards.

items.name: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park
items.text: About 344,000 km². The largest coral reef system in the world, a World Heritage Site since 1981.

items.name: Galápagos Islands
items.text: World Heritage Site since 1978, with a marine reserve and endemic species that shaped Darwin’s ideas.

items.name: Kaziranga National Park
items.text: Home to most of the world’s greater one-horned rhinoceroses; World Heritage Site since 1985.

items.name: Keoladeo National Park
items.text: Bharatpur’s wetland reserve; a Ramsar site and World Heritage Site famous for migratory waterbirds.

items.name: Kruger National Park
items.text: About 19,500 km². A national park since 1926 and a stronghold for the Big Five.

items.name: Ranthambore National Park
items.text: A tiger reserve of dry deciduous forest around a medieval fort.

items.name: Serengeti
items.text: Site of the Great Migration, with well over a million wildebeest moving with the rains.

items.name: Sundarbans
items.text: The largest mangrove forest in the world and a refuge of the Bengal tiger; World Heritage Site.

items.name: Yellowstone National Park
items.text: Established in 1872 and widely regarded as the first national park in the world.

items.name: Canal du Midi
items.text: About 240 km, completed in 1681, linking the Atlantic and the Mediterranean; World Heritage Site since 1996.

items.name: Corinth Canal
items.text: About 6.3 km, opened in 1893, cut through rock only about 21 m wide.

items.name: Erie Canal
items.text: Opened in 1825, about 584 km from the Hudson River to Lake Erie.

items.name: Ganga Canal (Upper)
items.text: Opened in 1854 to irrigate the Ganga–Yamuna doab from Haridwar.

items.name: Grand Canal
items.text: About 1,776 km from Beijing to Hangzhou, the longest artificial waterway in the world.

items.name: Indira Gandhi Canal
items.text: A canal system of roughly 650 km that carries Himalayan river water into the Thar Desert.

items.name: Kiel Canal
items.text: About 98 km, opened in 1895, joining the North Sea and the Baltic; one of the busiest artificial waterways.

items.name: Panama Canal
items.text: About 82 km, opened in 1914 and widened in 2016, using locks to cross the isthmus.

items.name: Suez Canal
items.text: About 193 km, opened in 1869, joining the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.
